RECONCILIATION AND CORRECTED FINAL HYPOTHESIS

== Source of the discrepancy ==
The "55–67%" figure in the previous draft came from the BLACK MALES dedup table (tier 0: 65.0%, tier 1: 55.6%, tier 2: 66.7%), while the adjacent sentence described the all-black primary sample, whose exact values are tier 0: 64.6%, tier 1: 57.9%, tier 2: 66.7%. My earlier table narration rounded these to "60/60/70", producing the apparent mismatch. The hypothesis text has been corrected to cite the PRIMARY sample (all black, deduplicated) throughout, with the males range noted separately.

== Verified percentages (from the exported tables, exact values) ==
Primary — all black, deduplicated (table_black_dedup_full.csv), % with 1996 wealth ≤ $0:
- Jailed, tiers 0/1/2: 64.6% (48), 57.9% (38), 66.7% (9) → range 58–67%.
- Never-jailed, tiers 0/1/2/3: 29.6% (756), 25.1% (793), 22.9% (205), 21.1% (587) → range 21–30%.
Black males, deduplicated (table_black_males_dedup.csv):
- Jailed, tiers 0/1/2: 65.0% (40), 55.6% (36), 66.7% (9) → range 56–67%.
- Never-jailed: 30.8%, 27.5%, 22.7%, 18.4% → range 18–31%.
Sensitivity, duplicates retained (table_black_sensitivity_dupes.csv): jailed tiers 0–2: 77.6%, 63.6%, 70.0%; never-jailed 54.8%, 27.6%, 23.3%, 21.3% — same conclusion (tier-0 never-jailed is higher here only because duplicate rows disproportionately carry zero wealth; directional pattern unchanged).

== CORRECTED FINAL NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS ==

"Among black NLSY79 respondents, being jailed between 1985 and 1994 is associated with a substantial and persistent loss of wealth, and the form of that loss depends on the respondent's economic starting point — operationalized as baseline 1985 composite wealth tier, which stands in for income level because the dataset contains no income variable. Black individuals who started with little or no wealth (1985 wealth below the 75th percentile, ≈$9,200) were driven to and trapped at zero net worth: median 1996 wealth among the jailed was $0 in every tier below the top, versus $5,000–$16,000 among otherwise comparable never-jailed peers, and 58–67% of jailed respondents in those tiers remained at ≤$0 wealth in 1996 (57.9% in the low tier, 64.6% among those starting with zero/negative wealth, 66.7% in the middle tier) versus only 21–30% of never-jailed peers. Among black men specifically — who account for 113 of the 124 jailed cases — the same trap is slightly sharper at the extremes (56–67% of jailed men in tiers 0–2 end at ≤$0 wealth vs 18–31% of never-jailed men). Black individuals who started in the top wealth tier (>≈$24,900 in 1985) largely avoided the zero-wealth trap (30.3% jailed vs 21.1% never-jailed ending at ≤$0) but suffered the largest absolute losses: median 1985→1996 wealth change of −$9,500 versus +$6,900 for never-jailed peers, with the divergence concentrated in the post-window period (1990→1996 median change of +$300 vs +$10,800 among black men). Regression estimates conditioning on baseline wealth tier and sex put the jailed-vs-never-jailed penalty in 1985→1996 wealth change at ≈−$34,000 in the lowest tier, growing to ≈−$65,000 in the highest tier (all p<0.001; signed-log outcomes −3.7 to −7.4 log-points, all p<0.05) — i.e., the absolute dollar penalty rises with starting wealth, while the relative devastation (collapse to zero) hits those who started with the least. The association is robust to retaining duplicate records; because jailed respondents were already poorer at baseline and incarceration is not randomly assigned, this is an association, not a causal effect."

All other elements — workflow, regression estimates, sensitivity check, tier definitions, and carried caveats (unverifiable residence-based ever_jailed construction; 1990 mid-window ambiguity; wealth-tier-as-income-proxy; small female/tier-2 cells; dedup decision) — are unchanged from the previously reviewed result.

payload.hypothesis: Among black NLSY79 respondents, jailing between 1985 and 1994 is associated with persistent wealth loss whose form depends on baseline economic position (1985 wealth tier as income proxy, since no income variable exists): those starting with little/no wealth (<≈$9,200) were trapped at zero net worth (median 1996 wealth $0 vs $5,000–$16,000 for never-jailed peers; 58–67% of jailed ending at ≤$0 in tiers 0–2 vs 21–30% of never-jailed; black men 56–67% vs 18–31%), while those starting in the top tier (>≈$24,900) avoided the zero trap (30.3% vs 21.1% at ≤$0) but took the largest absolute hits (median 1985→1996 change −$9,500 vs +$6,900). Regression-estimated jailed penalties rise with baseline tier (≈−$34k to ≈−$65k, all p<0.001); effect concentrated among black men (113/124 jailed) and in the post-window 1990→1996 period; robust to duplicate retention; association, not causation.
payload.workflow: Load & validate CSV (12,013×6, 0 missing, schema verified) → deduplicate (10,114 unique; black n=2,465, jailed 124) → define Δ_early/Δ_late/Δ_total (primary: 1990→1996 and 1985→1996) → baseline-1985 wealth tiers (≤0; ≤$5,400; ≤$9,200; >$24,899) as income proxy → tier×jailed median-trajectory tables for black-all/black-males (primary), black-females (small-n caveat), duplicates-retained sensitivity, white-male context → OLS with HC3 SEs: d_total and signed-log(d_total) ~ tier×ever_jailed+sex → export 5 tables and quantify natural-language hypothesis with verified percentages.
